words.def: the skill involved in making something beautiful or useful by hand
words.ex: Mass production has made many forms of traditional craftsmanship commercially unviable.

words.def: the process of things becoming the same or very similar, for example cultures around the world
words.ex: Some commentators fear the homogenisation of culture as global brands spread.

words.def: to bring something back into use or popularity
words.ex: Workshops for young people have helped revive interest in traditional weaving.

words.def: to keep something in its original state or protect it from being lost or damaged
words.ex: Governments should provide funding to preserve historic buildings for future generations.

words.def: a situation in which many different types of people or things are included
words.ex: Cultural diversity can make cities more creative and economically dynamic.

words.def: existing but impossible to touch, such as traditions, music or skills
words.ex: Oral storytelling is an example of intangible heritage that is easily lost.

words.def: a set of actions that is always performed in the same way, often as part of a ceremony
words.ex: Shared meals are a ritual that brings families together in almost every culture.

words.def: an object made by people in the past, especially one of historical or cultural interest
words.ex: Many artefacts were removed from their countries of origin during the colonial era.

words.def: the sharing of ideas, art and customs between people from different countries
words.ex: Student exchange programmes encourage cultural exchange and lasting international friendships.

words.def: a fixed, oversimplified idea about what a particular type of person or group is like
words.ex: Films that rely on national stereotypes can reinforce prejudice.

words.def: activities such as painting, music, theatre, dance and literature, considered as a group
words.ex: Public funding for the arts is often among the first areas cut during a recession.

words.def: a building or place that is important to a community's history and identity
words.ex: The old theatre was restored because it is regarded as a cultural landmark.

words.def: respected and followed because it has existed for a very long time
words.ex: Many families still follow the time-honoured tradition of gathering for a meal at festivals.

words.def: tourism involving very large numbers of people visiting the same popular places
words.ex: Mass tourism can overwhelm small historic towns that were never designed for crowds.

words.def: travel to natural areas that is organised so as to protect the environment and benefit local people
words.ex: Well-managed ecotourism can give communities a financial reason to protect wildlife.

words.def: a situation in which a place receives more visitors than it can cope with, harming residents and the environment
words.ex: Several popular cities have introduced visitor limits in response to overtourism.

words.def: a place that many people visit for pleasure
words.ex: The island has become a major tourist destination since the new airport opened.

words.def: the business of providing food, drink and accommodation, for example in hotels and restaurants
words.ex: The hospitality industry employs a large share of young and seasonal workers.

words.def: the money that a government or organisation receives, for example from tourism or taxes
words.ex: Tourism revenue can help fund the maintenance of historic sites.

words.def: the arrival of a large number of people or things at the same time
words.ex: The summer influx of visitors doubles the population of some coastal villages.

words.def: far away from the places that most tourists visit
words.ex: More travellers are seeking destinations off the beaten track to avoid crowds.
col: a village off the beaten track

words.def: a detailed plan of a journey, listing the places to be visited
words.ex: A flexible itinerary allows travellers to spend longer in places they enjoy.

words.def: happening or needed only at a particular time of year
words.ex: Seasonal employment in tourist areas leaves many workers without income in winter.

words.def: real and genuine, not a copy or a version made mainly for tourists
words.ex: Many travellers want an authentic experience of local life rather than a staged show.

words.def: the process of organising something mainly to make a profit, often at the cost of its quality or character
words.ex: The commercialisation of local festivals can strip them of their original meaning.

words.def: the largest number of visitors a place can receive without being damaged
words.ex: Authorities should assess the carrying capacity of fragile sites before promoting them.

words.def: a strong desire to travel and see new places
words.ex: Social media images of distant beaches have fuelled wanderlust among young adults.

words.def: to increase your knowledge and experience of the world
words.ex: Living abroad, even briefly, can broaden young people's horizons.

words.def: a feeling of confusion or anxiety that people may have when they experience a very different way of life
words.ex: International students often experience culture shock during their first months abroad.

words.def: a place that attracts many tourists and charges them too much for poor-quality goods or services
words.ex: The old harbour has become a tourist trap full of overpriced cafes.

words.def: a holiday organised by a company at a fixed price that includes travel and accommodation
words.ex: Package holidays have made foreign travel affordable for millions of families.

words.def: travelling a long distance, especially by plane
words.ex: Long-haul flights make up a disproportionate share of aviation emissions.

words.def: a holiday spent at home or in your own country instead of travelling abroad
words.ex: Rising air fares have made the staycation an attractive option for many families.
words.ar: عطلة داخلية (قضاء الإجازة في البلد نفسه)

words.def: based on observation, measurement or experiment rather than on theory alone
words.ex: Policy decisions should be supported by empirical evidence rather than assumptions.

words.def: an idea or explanation that is suggested and then tested through study or experiment
words.ex: The team designed a series of trials to test the hypothesis that sleep improves memory.

words.def: the evaluation of a researcher's work by other experts in the same field before it is published
words.ex: Peer review helps to ensure that published studies meet basic standards of quality.

words.def: a sum of money given by a government, university or organisation to pay for a particular research project
words.ex: Young scientists often spend months writing applications for research grants instead of doing research.

words.def: a carefully controlled test of a new medicine or treatment on people
words.ex: A new drug must pass several stages of clinical trials before it can be approved.
col: take part in a clinical trial

words.def: relating to whether something is morally right or wrong
words.ex: Gene editing raises serious ethical questions about where the limits of science should lie.

words.def: research carried out to increase understanding rather than to solve a specific practical problem
words.ex: Many practical inventions grew out of fundamental research whose uses were not obvious at first.

words.def: to repeat an experiment or study in order to check whether the same results are obtained
words.ex: If other laboratories cannot replicate a finding, it should be treated with caution.

words.def: the information or conclusions discovered as a result of research
words.ex: The findings suggest that even small changes in diet can affect long-term health.

words.def: completely new and making a very important discovery or development
words.ex: Her groundbreaking work on vaccines saved countless lives.

words.def: the investigation of outer space using spacecraft, satellites and telescopes
words.ex: Supporters of space exploration argue that it produces technologies with everyday uses.

words.def: the deliberate changing of the genes of a living thing in order to alter its characteristics
words.ex: Genetic engineering could produce crops that tolerate drought, but public acceptance remains low.

words.def: a factor that can change and that may affect the result of an experiment
words.ex: Researchers must control other variables so that they can isolate the effect of the treatment.

words.def: the number of people or items included in a study
words.ex: Because the sample size was so small, the results cannot be generalised to the whole population.

words.def: a connection between two things in which one changes when the other does, which does not necessarily mean one causes the other
words.ex: A correlation between screen use and poor sleep does not prove that one causes the other.

words.def: possible and practical to achieve
words.ex: The plan is technically feasible, but it may be too expensive to carry out on a large scale.

words.def: the general agreement among most scientists in a field on a particular question
words.ex: There is a strong scientific consensus that human activity is warming the planet.

words.def: to be one of the first people to develop or use a new idea, method or activity
words.ex: The university pioneered the use of robots in surgery.

words.def: done carefully, thoroughly and exactly, so that the results can be trusted
words.ex: Rigorous testing is required before any new medicine can be approved for public use.

words.def: the movement of highly skilled and educated people from one country to another where pay or conditions are better
words.ex: Low research budgets have caused a brain drain of young scientists to wealthier countries.

words.def: the system by which a government collects money from people and businesses to pay for public services
words.ex: Higher taxation on luxury goods could help fund free public transport.

words.def: money paid by a government to reduce the cost of a product or service, or to support an industry
words.ex: Subsidies for electric vehicles have made them affordable for many middle-income families.

words.def: the money a government spends on services such as education, health and defence
words.ex: Cuts in public spending tend to hit the poorest households hardest.

words.def: help, especially money, that the government gives to people who are poor, ill or unemployed
words.ex: A well-designed welfare system provides a safety net without discouraging people from working.

words.def: a period when a country's economy shrinks, trade and industry decline, and unemployment usually rises
words.ex: During a recession, young workers are often the first to lose their jobs.

words.def: a general rise in prices over time, which reduces how much money can buy
words.ex: High inflation reduces the real value of wages and savings.

words.def: the amount by which a government's spending is greater than its income in a year
words.ex: Governments may raise taxes or cut services in order to reduce a budget deficit.

words.def: the fact of being responsible for your decisions and actions and expected to explain them
words.ex: Publishing spending data increases the accountability of public officials.

words.def: a system of administration with many complicated rules and processes, often criticised for being slow
words.ex: Excessive bureaucracy can discourage people from starting small businesses.

words.def: dishonest or illegal behaviour by people in power, especially accepting money in return for favours
words.ex: Corruption diverts public money away from schools and hospitals.

words.def: an official rule, or the process of controlling an activity through rules
words.ex: Stronger regulation of the banking sector could help prevent another financial crisis.

words.def: relating to government income, taxes and spending
words.ex: Fiscal policy can be used to stimulate the economy during a downturn.

words.def: an increase in the amount of goods and services that an economy produces over time
words.ex: Economic growth does not automatically reduce poverty if its benefits are unevenly shared.

words.def: to officially give money, time or resources to a particular person or purpose
words.ex: Governments must decide how to allocate limited funds between healthcare and education.

words.def: the selling of a state-owned company or service to private owners
words.ex: Critics argue that the privatisation of public services such as railways can lead to higher fares.

words.def: a government policy of reducing public spending sharply in order to lower debt
words.ex: Years of austerity left many public services underfunded and short of staff.

words.def: the minimum level of income considered necessary to meet basic needs in a particular country
words.ex: Millions of people in work still live below the poverty line.
col: lift people above the poverty line

words.def: the lowest hourly pay that employers are legally allowed to pay their workers
words.ex: Raising the minimum wage can improve living standards, although some employers may hire fewer staff.

words.def: the part of the economy that is owned or controlled by the government, such as state schools and hospitals
words.ex: In several countries, public sector workers such as nurses and teachers have seen their pay fall in real terms.

words.def: the state of being successful, especially financially
words.ex: Long-term prosperity depends on investment in education and infrastructure.

words.def: a large company that operates in several countries
words.ex: Multinationals can bring jobs to developing countries, but profits often flow abroad.

words.def: paying another company, often in a cheaper country, to do work that was done inside the organisation
words.ex: The outsourcing of customer service jobs has cut costs but sometimes damaged quality.

words.def: international trade without taxes or other restrictions on imports and exports
words.ex: Free trade agreements have lowered the price of many consumer goods.

words.def: a situation in which countries or people depend on each other
words.ex: Global supply chains have created a high level of economic interdependence.

words.def: the series of businesses and processes involved in producing a product and delivering it to customers
words.ex: A disruption at a single port can affect supply chains around the world.

words.def: a tax charged by a government on goods coming into or leaving a country
words.ex: Raising tariffs on imported steel may protect local jobs but increase costs for manufacturers.

words.def: a country whose economy is developing quickly and becoming more involved in global markets
words.ex: Emerging economies now account for a growing share of world trade.

words.def: the unfair treatment of people, especially paying them very little for their work
words.ex: Consumers increasingly demand proof that their clothes were not made through the exploitation of workers.

words.def: a factory or workshop where people work very long hours for very low pay in poor conditions
words.ex: Media investigations have exposed sweatshop conditions in factories supplying well-known fashion brands.
words.ar: مصنع استغلالي (أجور زهيدة وظروف عمل قاسية)

words.def: happening between different countries or involving people from different countries
words.ex: Cross-border cooperation is essential for tackling pandemics and climate change.

words.def: the policy of protecting a country's industries from foreign competition by taxing or restricting imports
words.ex: A rise in protectionism could slow the growth of global trade.

words.def: people who move to another region or country in order to find work
words.ex: Migrant workers often send a large part of their earnings back to their families.

words.def: money sent home by people working in another country
words.ex: In some countries, remittances are worth more than all foreign aid combined.

words.def: the idea that the world has become like one small community because of modern communications
words.ex: The internet has turned the world into a global village in which news travels instantly.

words.def: a government rule, such as a tax or quota, that makes trade between countries more difficult
words.ex: Removing trade barriers can benefit consumers but expose local farmers to fierce competition.

words.def: a language used for communication between people who have different first languages
words.ex: English has become the lingua franca of international business and science.

words.def: the process of combining economies or societies so that they work closely together
words.ex: Closer regional integration has made it easier for businesses to sell across borders.

words.def: located or operating in another country, often to reduce costs or taxes
words.ex: Some firms move production offshore to take advantage of lower labour costs.

words.def: money that companies or individuals from one country put into businesses or projects in another
words.ex: In many developing countries, foreign investment has helped build new factories and transport links.

words.def: the spread of one powerful country's culture, values and products at the expense of local cultures
words.ex: Some critics regard the global dominance of a few film studios as cultural imperialism.

words.def: buses, trains and other services that are available for everyone to use, usually for a fare
words.ex: Cheap and reliable public transport is one of the most effective ways to reduce car use in cities.

words.def: to travel regularly between home and work or study
words.ex: Many employees now commute only two or three days a week.

words.def: (of an area, a day or a lifestyle) without private cars, or where cars are not allowed
words.ex: Car-free days give residents a chance to rediscover their streets on foot and by bicycle.

words.def: a fee that drivers must pay to enter a busy area, such as a city centre, at certain times
words.ex: Revenue from a congestion charge can be reinvested in cycle lanes and better bus services.

words.def: designed in a way that makes it hard to live or travel without a car
words.ex: Car-dependent suburbs make life difficult for older people who can no longer drive.

words.def: the prevention of accidents and injuries on roads
words.ex: Lower speed limits near schools are a simple way to improve road safety.

words.def: how far a vehicle can travel using a given amount of fuel
words.ex: Stricter standards for fuel efficiency have reduced emissions from new cars.

words.def: a vehicle powered by an electric motor and a rechargeable battery instead of petrol or diesel
words.ex: The spread of electric vehicles depends on a reliable network of charging points.

words.def: a railway system on which trains travel much faster than on conventional lines
words.ex: High-speed rail could replace many short domestic flights.

words.def: a part of a road or a separate path reserved for bicycles
words.ex: Protected cycle lanes encourage more people to cycle to work safely.

words.def: the fact of owning a car, or the proportion of people or households that own one
words.ex: In many fast-growing cities, rising car ownership has outpaced the construction of new roads.

words.def: an arrangement in which people share a car for regular journeys, such as to work
words.ex: Carpooling reduces both fuel costs and the number of vehicles on the road.

words.def: a system in which drivers leave their cars in car parks on the edge of a town and travel into the centre by bus or tram
words.ex: A park-and-ride scheme could keep thousands of cars out of the historic centre every day.
words.ar: نظام «اركن واركب» (مواقف على أطراف المدينة مع نقل إلى وسطها)

words.def: easy for everyone, including disabled people, older people and parents with pushchairs, to reach, enter or use
words.ex: Every new station should be fully accessible to wheelchair users and parents with young children.

words.def: an area of a city that the most polluting vehicles may not enter, or must pay to enter
words.ex: Since the low-emission zone was introduced, levels of harmful gases around nearby schools have fallen.

words.def: goods carried by trains, ships, planes or lorries
words.ex: Moving more freight from road to rail would cut both congestion and pollution.

words.def: a vehicle that can drive itself without a human controlling it
words.ex: Autonomous vehicles could reduce accidents caused by human error, but legal questions remain.

words.def: measures such as speed bumps, narrower roads and raised crossings that are designed to slow vehicles down, especially in residential areas
words.ex: Traffic calming measures outside schools have made the streets safer for children walking to class.

words.def: a situation in which traffic is so heavy that vehicles cannot move at all
words.ex: A single accident on the ring road can bring the city to gridlock.

words.def: a change in the way people travel, for example from cars to public transport or bicycles
words.ex: A modal shift from private cars to trains is essential for meeting climate goals.

words.def: a situation in which everyone has reliable access to enough safe and nutritious food
words.ex: Climate change poses a serious threat to food security in regions that rely on rain-fed crops.

words.def: (of food or farming) produced without artificial chemicals such as synthetic fertilisers or pesticides
words.ex: Organic produce is usually more expensive, partly because yields per hectare tend to be lower.

words.def: a chemical used to kill insects or other pests that damage crops
words.ex: Heavy pesticide use has been linked to declining numbers of bees.

words.def: the amount of a crop produced from a given area of land
words.ex: New irrigation methods have helped farmers raise crop yields without using more water.

words.def: (of a plant or animal) having had its genes changed in a laboratory to give it particular features
words.ex: Genetically modified crops can resist certain pests, but many consumers remain wary of them.

words.def: farming that uses a lot of machinery, chemicals and animals or crops on limited land to maximise production
words.ex: Intensive farming produces cheap food but can damage soil and water quality.

words.def: animals such as cows, sheep and goats that are kept on a farm
words.ex: Producing food from livestock generally requires far more land and water than producing the same number of calories from crops.

words.def: food that is thrown away instead of being eaten
words.ex: Supermarkets could cut food waste by donating unsold items to charities.

words.def: food that has been changed by industrial methods, often with added salt, sugar or preservatives
words.ex: Diets high in processed food are associated with higher rates of heart disease.
col: a diet high in processed food

words.def: poor health caused by not eating enough food or not eating the right kinds of food
words.ex: Malnutrition in early childhood can affect brain development for life.

words.def: able to produce everything you need without help from others, for example all the food a country eats
words.ex: Few countries are fully self-sufficient in food, so international trade remains essential.

words.def: supplying water to land or crops through channels, pipes or sprinklers
words.ex: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots and greatly reduces waste.

words.def: (of land) suitable for growing crops
words.ex: Urban expansion is swallowing up arable land around many fast-growing cities.

words.def: a basic food that forms the main part of a population's diet, such as rice, wheat or maize
words.ex: Price rises in staple foods hit the poorest families hardest.

words.def: the distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
words.ex: Buying seasonal local produce reduces food miles.
words.ar: المسافة التي يقطعها الغذاء (من المزرعة إلى المستهلك)

words.def: (of food or a diet) made mainly or only from plants, not animal products
words.ex: A shift towards plant-based diets could significantly reduce agricultural emissions.

words.def: a natural or chemical substance added to soil to help plants grow
words.ex: Run-off from chemical fertilisers can cause harmful algae to spread in lakes.

words.def: a situation in which a large number of people do not have enough food for a long period, often causing many deaths
words.ex: Early warning systems can help governments prevent drought from turning into famine.

words.def: farming and food production run as a large-scale industry by big companies
words.ex: Small farmers often struggle to compete with large agribusiness firms.

words.def: the gradual loss of the top layer of soil, caused by wind, water or poor farming practices
words.ex: Planting hedgerows can help prevent soil erosion on exposed farmland.

linking.example: Cycling to work saves money on fuel. Moreover, it builds regular exercise into people's daily routine.
linking.tip: Use these to add a point that supports the same argument. Put a comma after a linker that opens a sentence (Moreover, Furthermore,). Do not start every sentence with one: mechanical linking is noticed by examiners and can lower your Coherence and Cohesion score. 'as well as' is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not a full clause.
linking.tipAr: تُستخدم لإضافة فكرة تدعم الحجّة نفسها. ضع فاصلة بعد الرابط إذا جاء في بداية الجملة، مثل: Moreover, وFurthermore,. ولا تبدأ كل جملة برابط؛ فالمصحّح يلاحظ الربط الآلي المتكرّر، وقد يُخفّض ذلك درجتك في معيار الترابط والتماسك. ويأتي بعد as well as اسمٌ أو فعلٌ بصيغة ing، لا جملة كاملة.

linking.example: Urban households tend to rent their homes, whereas rural families are more likely to own property.
linking.tip: 'whereas' and 'while' join two contrasting clauses inside one sentence. 'However' and 'In contrast' normally begin a new sentence and are followed by a comma. Never join two complete sentences with only a comma and 'however': use a full stop or a semicolon before it. 'On the other hand' should follow a point you have already made; 'Conversely' means the opposite relationship is true, so it is not simply another word for 'however'.
linking.tipAr: تربط whereas وwhile بين فكرتين متقابلتين داخل جملة واحدة. أمّا However وIn contrast فتبدأ بهما عادةً جملة جديدة وتليهما فاصلة. ولا تربط جملتين تامّتين بفاصلة وحدها ثم however، بل ضع قبلها نقطة أو فاصلة منقوطة. واستخدم On the other hand بعد أن تعرض الفكرة الأولى، واعلم أن Conversely تعني أن العلاقة معكوسة، فليست مجرد مرادف لـ However.

linking.example: Although online courses are cheaper, many learners find it difficult to stay motivated without face-to-face contact.
linking.tip: Conceding shows that you can weigh both sides before giving your view, which is useful in opinion essays. 'Despite' and 'In spite of' are followed by a noun or an -ing form (despite the cost; despite being expensive), never by a subject and a verb. Do not use 'although' and 'but' in the same sentence.
linking.tipAr: يُظهر التسليم بالرأي المقابل أنك توازن بين الجانبين قبل أن تعرض رأيك، وهذا مفيد في مقالات الرأي. يأتي بعد Despite وIn spite of اسمٌ أو فعلٌ بصيغة ing (مثل: despite the cost)، ولا تأتي بعدهما جملة فيها فاعل وفعل. ولا تجمع although وbut في جملة واحدة؛ وهذا خطأ شائع لدى متحدثي العربية لأننا نقول: «مع أنّ... إلا أنّ».

items: The main reason for this is that
linking.example: Many young people delay buying a home because of rising property prices.
linking.tip: 'because' is followed by a clause (because prices have risen), while 'because of', 'due to' and 'owing to' are followed by a noun phrase (because of rising prices). 'Due to' is safest after the verb 'be' (The delay was due to bad weather). A sentence such as 'Because it is cheaper.' on its own is incomplete: it needs a main clause.
linking.tipAr: يأتي بعد because جملةٌ كاملة (because prices have risen)، أمّا because of وdue to وowing to فيليها اسم أو عبارة اسمية (because of rising prices). والاستعمال الأسلم لـ due to يكون بعد فعل الكينونة be (The delay was due to bad weather). ولا تكتب جملة مثل: Because it is cheaper. وحدها، فهي ناقصة تحتاج إلى جملة رئيسية.

linking.example: Housing in the city centre has become unaffordable. As a result, many key workers now commute long distances.
linking.tip: 'so' joins two clauses inside one sentence, usually with a comma before it. 'Therefore', 'Consequently' and 'As a result' normally start a new sentence or follow a semicolon. 'Thus' is formal, so use it sparingly. Check that the second idea really is a result of the first: a linker that does not match the logic weakens your writing.
linking.tipAr: تربط so بين جملتين داخل جملة واحدة وتسبقها فاصلة عادةً، أمّا Therefore وConsequently وAs a result فتبدأ بها عادةً جملة جديدة أو تأتي بعد فاصلة منقوطة. وThus كلمة رسمية فاستخدمها باعتدال. وتأكّد أن الفكرة الثانية نتيجة فعلية للأولى؛ فالرابط الذي لا يوافق منطق الكلام يُضعف كتابتك.

linking.example: Many everyday products, such as smartphones and laptops, contain rare metals that are difficult to recycle.
linking.tip: 'such as' and 'including' are followed by nouns, not full sentences, and do not need 'etc.' at the end. 'For example' and 'For instance' can open a sentence, followed by a comma. In Task 2, a short, specific example from general knowledge or experience is more convincing than an invented statistic or a made-up study.
linking.tipAr: يأتي بعد such as وincluding أسماءٌ لا جمل كاملة، ولا حاجة إلى كتابة etc. بعدها. ويمكن أن تبدأ الجملة بـ For example أو For instance مع فاصلة بعدهما. وفي المهمة الثانية يكون المثال القصير المحدّد من المعرفة العامة أو التجربة أقوى إقناعًا من إحصائية مختلَقة أو دراسة وهمية.

linking.example: First, the harvested olives are washed. Once they have been crushed into a paste, the oil is separated from the water, after which it is filtered and bottled.
linking.tip: Essential for process diagrams in Academic Task 1 and for describing steps in Speaking. Vary the structure with patterns such as 'Once the leaves have dried, ...', 'after which ...' and 'before being ...'. In essays, avoid opening every paragraph with 'Firstly', 'Secondly', 'Thirdly': these organise the text but do not show how the ideas are related.
linking.tipAr: ضرورية لوصف مخططات المراحل (Process) في المهمة الأولى الأكاديمية، ولوصف الخطوات في اختبار المحادثة. نوّع التراكيب، مثل: Once the leaves have dried و after which و before being. وفي المقالات تجنّب أن تبدأ كل فقرة بـ Firstly ثم Secondly ثم Thirdly؛ فهذه الكلمات ترتّب النص لكنها لا تبيّن العلاقة بين الأفكار.

linking.example: Many graduates are underemployed; in other words, they work in jobs that do not require a degree.
linking.tip: Use these to explain a complex or abstract idea in simpler terms. In formal writing, prefer 'in other words' or 'that is to say' to abbreviations such as 'i.e.'. Do not use them to repeat the same point just to reach the word count: examiners recognise repetition.
linking.tipAr: تُستخدم لشرح فكرة معقّدة أو مجرّدة بكلمات أبسط. وفي الكتابة الرسمية فضّل in other words أو that is to say على الاختصارات مثل i.e. ولا تستخدمها لتكرار الفكرة نفسها بهدف بلوغ عدد الكلمات؛ فالمصحّح يكتشف التكرار.

linking.example: Teenagers today spend more time online than their parents did at the same age. Similarly, they are more likely to make friends through social media.
linking.tip: Comparison is a key requirement in Academic Task 1: combine these with comparatives and structures such as 'twice as many ... as' and 'the highest proportion'. 'Similarly' and 'Likewise' show that two things share a feature; they cannot introduce a difference. Watch the prepositions: 'the same as' (not 'the same like') and 'similar to' (not 'similar with').
linking.tipAr: المقارنة مطلب أساسي في المهمة الأولى الأكاديمية، فاستخدم هذه الروابط مع صيغ التفضيل وتراكيب مثل twice as many ... as وthe highest proportion. أمّا Similarly وLikewise فتدلّان على التشابه، ولا تُستخدمان لعرض اختلاف. وانتبه إلى حروف الجر: the same as لا the same like، وsimilar to لا similar with.

linking.example: On balance, the benefits of a shorter working week appear to outweigh the risks.
linking.tip: Use one concluding phrase, at the start of the final paragraph of an essay, and restate your position without adding new arguments. In Academic Task 1, 'Overall,' introduces the overview of the main features; it can follow the introduction or come at the end, as long as it is clearly there. Avoid informal phrases such as 'In a nutshell' or 'To wrap up' in formal writing.
linking.tipAr: استخدم عبارة ختامية واحدة في بداية الفقرة الأخيرة من المقال، وأكّد فيها موقفك دون إضافة حجج جديدة. وفي المهمة الأولى الأكاديمية تُقدِّم Overall الملخص العام لأبرز السمات، ويمكن أن يأتي بعد المقدمة مباشرة أو في النهاية، على أن يكون واضحًا. وتجنّب العبارات غير الرسمية مثل In a nutshell وTo wrap up في الكتابة الرسمية.

task1.use: Trends: a gradual, continuous increase. Give the start and end figures. Vary it with 'climbed', 'grew' or the noun form 'a steady rise in'.
Trends: a sudden, large decrease. 'plummeted' is stronger and suits only very dramatic drops, so do not use it for small changes.
Trends: little or no change over a period. 'relatively' and 'around' keep the claim accurate when the line moves slightly.
Trends: repeated rises and falls with no clear direction. Give the range rather than describing every small movement.
Trends: the highest point of a line. Pair it with what happened next, e.g. 'peaked at 45% in 2010 before declining'.
Trends: the lowest point. 'reached a low of' is a more neutral alternative.
Trends: a rise or fall that stops and stays flat. Useful for describing the final years of a period.

task1.en: there was a dramatic rise in ...
task1.use: Trends: the noun pattern (there was + adjective + noun + in) lets you vary your sentences instead of repeating 'X increased'.
Trends and comparisons: shows a multiple instead of listing two numbers. Only use 'doubled' or 'tripled' when the figures support it.
Trends: future data in a graph. Use 'is expected to', 'is predicted to' or 'is forecast to', never 'will reach' as if it were certain.

task1.en: was significantly higher than that of ...
task1.use: Comparison: 'that of' / 'those of' prevents a common error, comparing a figure with a country rather than with another figure.
Comparison: multiples. Use 'many' with countable nouns (people, cars) and 'much' with uncountable ones (energy, water).
Comparison: emphasises a category that is much bigger than all the others. Use it once per answer for the most striking feature.
Comparison over time: when one line crosses another. This is often a key feature worth mentioning in your overview.

task1.en: the gap between ... and ... widened / narrowed
task1.use: Comparison over time: describes a difference that grows or shrinks. A good way to compare two lines in a single sentence.
Comparison: very small differences. 'slightly' is a simpler alternative; avoid exaggerating small gaps.
Comparison: ordering categories in bar charts and tables without listing every value.
Proportions: the share of a total in pie charts and tables. 'made up' and 'represented' are good alternatives.
Proportions: approximate fractions (just over half, roughly a third, nearly two-thirds). Use them with the exact figure, not instead of it, when accuracy matters.
Proportions: very large shares, about 80% or more. The opposite is 'a small minority of'. Do not write 'most of people'.

task1.en: made up the largest share of ...
task1.use: Proportions: identifies the biggest segment of a pie chart. Follow it with the figure in brackets or a short clause.

task1.en: the proportion of ... who ... rose from ... to ...
task1.use: Proportions over time: makes clear that you are describing a percentage, not a number. Do not mix up 'proportion' and 'number'.

task1.en: The chart compares ... in terms of ...
task1.use: Introduction: paraphrase the task in one sentence using your own words. Copied wording from the question is not credited.

task1.en: Overall, the most noticeable feature is ...
task1.use: Overview: every Task 1 answer needs a clear summary of the main features. Avoid starting every overview with 'It is clear that'.

task1.en: The process consists of ... stages, beginning with ... and ending with ...
task1.use: Processes: a concise overview stating the number of stages and the first and last steps.

task1.en: ... is then transported to ..., where it is ...
task1.use: Processes: the passive voice is natural because the focus is on the material, not on who does the action. Vary 'then' with 'next' and 'subsequently'.
Processes: links two stages in one sentence and shows the order clearly. A good alternative to starting every sentence with 'Next'.

task1.en: was demolished to make way for ...
task1.use: Maps: a building removed and replaced by something new. Use the past simple passive for changes between two dates.
Maps: a change of use, for example a factory converted into flats. 'was turned into' is a slightly less formal alternative.

task1.en: to the north of ... / in the south-eastern corner of ...
task1.use: Maps: precise location. Compass directions are clearer than 'on the top' or 'at the left' of the map.

task2.en: I firmly believe that ...
task2.use: Position: states a clear opinion in the introduction of an opinion essay. Restate it in different words in the conclusion rather than repeating the same phrase.

task2.en: I agree with this view to a large extent, although ...
task2.use: Position: partial agreement with a limit. Only use it if your body paragraphs really reflect both sides.

task2.en: This essay will argue that ...
task2.use: Position: a direct thesis statement. Avoid long memorised openings such as 'This is a controversial issue that has sparked heated debate'; examiners recognise them and give them no credit.

task2.en: In my view, the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
task2.use: Position: answers 'Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?' directly. Make sure your paragraphs show why one side is stronger.

task2.en: While this argument has some merit, ...
task2.use: Position: concedes the opposing view before rejecting it. Use it once; repeated concessions make your position unclear.

task2.en: Opponents of this view argue that ...
task2.use: Discussion essays: introduces the other side's argument neutrally before you evaluate it.

task2.en: is likely to ...
task2.use: Hedging: makes a prediction sound reasonable rather than certain. Stronger: 'is almost certain to'; weaker: 'may well'.

task2.en: tends to ...
task2.use: Hedging: generalises carefully (Young people tend to ...). Safer than absolute statements such as 'All young people ...'.

task2.en: It could be argued that ...
task2.use: Hedging: presents a view without fully committing to it. Do not overuse it, or your own position will seem unclear.

task2.en: to some extent / in many cases
task2.use: Hedging: limits the scope of a claim. Place it close to the idea it limits.

task2.en: There is some evidence that ...
task2.use: Hedging: refers to general knowledge carefully. Do not invent precise statistics or studies to support your argument.

task2.en: A clear example of this is ...
task2.use: Examples: introduces a specific, relevant example after a general point. One well-explained example is better than a list of three.

task2.en: This can be seen in ..., where ...
task2.use: Examples: links an example to a real place or situation and explains it in the same sentence.

task2.en: Take, for instance, ...
task2.use: Examples: a slightly more formal way to begin an example sentence. Use it once per essay at most.

task2.en: This would mean that ...
task2.use: Development: explains the consequence of an idea. Extending ideas this way is key to a higher Task Response score.

task2.en: One major drawback of ... is that ...
task2.use: Advantages/disadvantages and positive/negative essays: introduces a disadvantage. Vary it with 'A further concern is that ...'.

task2.en: A more effective solution would be to ...
task2.use: Problem-solution essays: proposes a solution and suggests it is better than the alternatives. Explain how it would work, not just what it is.

task2.en: The root of the problem lies in ...
task2.use: Problem-solution essays: introduces a cause. Make sure each solution you offer matches a cause or problem you have identified.

task2.en: In conclusion, although ..., I remain convinced that ...
task2.use: Conclusion: summarises your position and acknowledges the other side in one sentence. Do not introduce new arguments here.

task2.en: For these reasons, governments should ...
task2.use: Conclusion: ends with a clear recommendation, especially in problem-solution essays. Keep it consistent with the rest of the essay.

speaking.en: I haven't really thought about that before, but I suppose ...
speaking.use: Buying time: gives you a moment to think, especially in Part 3. Avoid the overused opener 'That's an interesting question', and use this kind of phrase only once or twice in the test; repeated stock phrases sound memorised.

speaking.en: Let me think about that for a second ...
speaking.use: Buying time: honest and natural. Follow it quickly with an answer; long silences affect fluency.

speaking.en: It's hard to say, really, but I suppose ...
speaking.use: Buying time and hedging: useful for abstract Part 3 questions where you are not sure of your view.

speaking.en: Off the top of my head, I'd say ...
speaking.use: Buying time: informal and natural in Part 1, meaning you are giving a quick answer without much thought.
Buying time: signals that you are searching for the right words. Use it sparingly.

speaking.en: Sorry, could you repeat the question, please?
speaking.use: Clarifying: perfectly acceptable and not penalised. In Part 1 the examiner can only repeat the question; in Part 3 the examiner can rephrase it.
Opinions: a softer, more natural alternative to 'I think' in all parts of the test.

speaking.en: Personally, I'm a big fan of ...
speaking.use: Opinions: expresses a strong personal liking, which suits Part 1 questions about hobbies and preferences.

speaking.en: I'm not really into ..., to be honest.
speaking.use: Opinions: a natural way to say you do not like something. Then explain why or say what you prefer instead.
Opinions: slightly more formal, suitable for Part 3. Do not repeat the same opinion phrase in every answer.

speaking.en: I can see both sides, but on the whole I think ...
speaking.use: Opinions: shows balanced thinking in Part 3 discussion questions while still giving a clear view.
Opinions: a strong Part 3 answer pattern, as long as you explain what it depends on. 'It depends' alone is not an answer.
Adding detail: extends a short answer with a reason. In Part 1, an answer plus one reason or example is usually enough.
Clarifying yourself: rephrase an idea when you feel it came out unclear. Self-correction like this is a sign of good fluency, not a weakness.
Adding detail: a personal example with a past tense adds grammar range and makes your answer more convincing.
Adding detail: an informal way to add a second point, more natural in speech than 'Moreover'.
Adding detail: emphasises an additional point in a lively way.
Adding detail: generalises and contrasts in one sentence, which suits Part 3 questions about society.

speaking.en: Compared to when I was a child, ...
speaking.use: Adding detail: compares past and present, a natural way to use a range of tenses in Part 3.
Rounding off: ends an answer naturally by linking back to the question, instead of stopping abruptly or saying 'That's all'.
